newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi under fire over mini-budget.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi under fire over mini-budget.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi ran into trouble from the opposition and even his own coalition allies on Thursday after announcing he would pass a mini-budget to ensure Italy was in shape to help found a European single currency.

Economic commentators, echoing the fears of ordinary Italians, wondered where Prodi was going to find the cash for fresh cuts in a runaway deficit just two months after passing a 1997 budget. He has already promised no new taxes.
"It's time to leave ambiguity behind" urged financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore in an editorial as Prodi's difficulties mounted.
"The (ruling) majority must choose a precise line and show its cohesion, if it has any," the newspaper said.
Prodi's sudden decision to go ahead with the much-rumoured mini-budget after turbulence on financial markets exposed simmering strains within his ruling centre-left coalition.

Massimo D'Alema, whose Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) is the biggest in the nine-month-old government told reporters on Monday that a mini-budget was inevitable but Prodi retorted within hours that no decision had been made.

When, on Wednesday, Prodi said he had made up his mind to pass a mini-budget after all, the PDS cried foul, complaining it had not been consulted and demanding an urgent meeting to clarify what measures the mini-budget's would contain.

Prodi has said he will wait until official accounts are out next month before detailing the size and scope of the mini-budget, but newspapers expected it to seek a "contribution" from pensioners, changes in severance pay, health cuts, a rise in the cost of petrol and cigarettes and possibly in sales tax.
The plan sparked instant criticism from hardline Communist Refoundation whose support gives Prodi a parliamentary majority.
The party's leader, Fausto Bertinotti, laid down twin conditions -- no spending cuts, no new taxes -- for its support.
Oppposition centre-right Freedom Alliance leader Silvio Berlusconi on Thursday tied support for the budget to a deal to cut welfare spending, warning Prodi he was "playing with fire".
Union leaders have also attacked the plan. "If any cuts are proposed, we will refuse," said Sergio D'Antoni, leader of the big CISL trades union confederation on Thursday.
"Cuts would open up a social conflict of unheard of proportions. It is impossible," he told reporters.
Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni used a speech to a PDS congress to insist that it would be "extremely grave and irresponsible" not to pass a mini-budget.
But Il Sole said it was time the government stopped coming up with budgets that it said were "adequate", only to have to pass supplementary measures months or even weeks later.

The 1997 budget contains measures to cut 62.5 trillion lire ($37.3 billion) off this year's deficit and was supposed to ensure Italy met a key three percent ratio of deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) required for economic and monetary union.
The government was forced into a mini-budget after a deficit overshoot last year. The package, due within weeks, is expected to contain measures to cut the deficit by 13-15 trillion lire.
Il Sole urged Prodi not to resort to one-off measures, like the controversial "Euro-tax" contained in the 1997 budget. The EU is due to rule on Friday on whether the levy is permissable.

"The only action which can avoid highly damaging financial instability is...incisive and sustainable structural reforms, avoiding acrobatics based on future and uncertain macroeconomic factors," Il Sole said. ($1=1,672 lire)
